q: Three warm days pass with nobody touching a red fermenter, and the top of the cap dries out in the air. What is the specific danger sitting in that crust?
opts: Brettanomyces breeds in the crust and drains back as a sweeter second wine
Acetic bacteria colonise the exposed skins and raise volatile acidity
Film yeast spread across the dry crust and leave the wine a shade paler
The dried skins take up the wine's alcohol, so the red falls short of its strength
exp: Skins above the liquid are warm, wet with sugar and open to the air, which is precisely the habitat acetic bacteria want. Keeping the cap submerged or at least wet is therefore a preservation job as much as an extraction one, and the volatile acidity a neglected crust throws cannot be taken back out of the wine afterwards.

q: Slatted boards hold the skins permanently below the surface of a fermenting red, so no crust ever forms at all. How does extraction under that arrangement compare?
opts: Colour is extracted but tannin is not
Slow and steady, with no aeration and no daily cap work
Fast and hard, because the skins are held under pressure
Almost nothing is extracted, since the skins are never agitated
exp: A submerged cap keeps every skin in contact with wine at all times and needs no plunging, which suits a cellar without the hands for three punch-downs a day. It also shuts out air, so wines raised this way often want aeration later on.

q: Juice is bled off a red fermenter after a few hours on the skins and finished separately as a pink wine. Beside a rose pressed straight from red grapes, how does that wine usually show?
opts: Deeper in colour and fuller in body
Indistinguishable, since both come from the same fruit
Paler and lighter, with lower alcohol
Sweeter, because the juice never ferments out
exp: The bled juice comes off a vat set up to make red wine, from riper fruit and with more skin contact than fruit picked and pressed for pink in the first place. Saignee is the word for the bleeding, and a dark example is easily mistaken for a light red on the table.

q: Colour climbs steeply in a red fermenter for the first several days and then starts to fall back, although the skins are still sitting in the wine. What accounts for the decline?
opts: Escaping carbon dioxide carries the pigment up and out of the tank
The rising temperature of the vat bleaches the pigment out
The pigment ferments away into alcohol along with the sugar
Pigment binds to skins, seeds and yeast and drops out of solution
exp: Anthocyanins are adsorbed by the solids in the vat and by the yeast themselves, so a longer maceration does not automatically mean a darker wine. It is one of the reasons a cellar tastes a fermenter daily rather than working to a fixed number of days.

q: Inside an unbroken berry sealed under carbon dioxide, the fruit's own enzymes go to work before any yeast can reach the pulp. Which acid is largely consumed in that process?
opts: Acetic acid
Tartaric acid
Malic acid
Lactic acid
exp: Intracellular fermentation burns off much of the berry's malic acid and makes a small amount of alcohol along with the perfumed aromatics the method is prized for. Losing that acid is why such wines taste soft and round while still very young, even off fruit picked at modest ripeness.

q: Red must is run through a heat exchanger at seventy degrees, held there for two hours and then pressed before any yeast is pitched. What is the cellar buying with that heat?
opts: A firmer tannin structure than a long maceration on the skins could build
A higher final alcohol, since the heat drives water off and concentrates the sugar in the must
Colour out of the skins in hours, with the wine then fermented off them like a white
A wine that will age longer in bottle than one fermented on its skins in the usual way
exp: Heat pulls pigment out of the skins in a couple of hours, so the juice can be pressed off and fermented clear like a white, and the press house is free again the same day. What comes back is colour and soft fruit with very little tannin, which is why thermovinification belongs to volume reds meant to be drunk young. It is also reached for when rot has left an enzyme in the fruit that would otherwise brown the wine, since the heat destroys it.

q: A vat is filled with destemmed but deliberately uncrushed berries and left to break down gradually under their own weight. What is the winemaker expecting to gain?
opts: A higher final alcohol than the same fruit crushed would reach
A ferment that runs right through to dryness in three days
A gentler start, brighter fruit and softer tannin
A deeper colour than crushing the fruit would have given
exp: Whole berries ferment partly from the inside as their skins give way, which is slower and less extractive than working a fully crushed must. It is a common choice with thin-skinned varieties where the aim is perfume and lift rather than density.

q: A cool-vintage must reads ten and a half degrees of potential alcohol, and a measured weight of beet sugar is stirred in before fermentation. What does the finished wine gain, and what does it not?
opts: Alcohol and sweetness both, since some of the sugar survives
Sweetness and body, but no extra alcohol, since none of it ferments
Alcohol and body, but no sweetness, since the yeast ferment it away
Colour and tannin, but no gain in alcohol at all
exp: Chaptalisation gives the yeast more sugar to work with, so the wine finishes stronger and drier rather than sweeter. It cannot make unripe fruit taste ripe, which is why it is treated as a correction to a hard year and not as a recipe.

q: Fruit picked in a hot year comes in at pH 3.9 and the juice tastes soft and flat. Which addition is the standard remedy in cellars permitted to make it?
opts: Potassium sorbate
Tartaric acid
Calcium carbonate
Beet sugar
exp: Tartaric is chosen because the grape already contains it and, unlike malic, bacteria will not consume it later, so the correction holds. Dropping the pH also sharpens the finish and makes whatever sulphur dioxide is in the wine far more effective as a preservative.

q: A cool northern white finishes with acidity so sharp it is painful to taste, and the cellar wants to blunt it before bottling. Which treatment does that job?
opts: Adding tartaric acid, which binds the sharp acid and drops it out
Warming the wine gently in tank until part of the acid is driven off
Stirring in a chalk-based salt that drops part of the acid out
Sweetening the wine with a measure of grape spirit before bottling
exp: Calcium carbonate reacts with the acid and drops out as an insoluble salt that is filtered away, so total acidity falls and the wine reads rounder. Deacidification is much rarer worldwide than acidification, since only cool regions in poor years ever need it.

q: A finished red reads sixteen and a half per cent and burns on the finish, and the producer wants it nearer fourteen without cooking the wine. Which treatment answers that?
opts: Filtering the wine through a pad fine enough to hold the alcohol back
Chilling the wine until the alcohol freezes out and is skimmed off
Reverse osmosis, taking the alcohol out of what crosses the membrane
Adding water to the tank until the reading falls, without thinning it
exp: The membrane separates a thin watery fraction from the wine, the alcohol is taken out of that fraction alone, and what is left goes back, which is why the flavour survives the operation. A spinning cone reaches the same end by vacuum distillation at a temperature low enough not to cook anything. Simply watering a wine back from sixteen and a half to fourteen would take something like a seventh of its volume in water, which hollows the wine out even where the law allows it.

q: A thin, hollow red is dosed before ageing with a powder extracted from grape skins, seeds and oak. What is that addition there to do?
opts: Add structure and help hold the colour in place
Raise the alcohol, since the powder carries sugar too
Strip bitterness out of a coarse young red
Lower the pH, so the wine finishes fresher
exp: Oenological tannin binds with pigment and helps fix colour as well as building grip on the palate. It cannot invent concentration, so it works at the margin of a weak wine rather than transforming one.

q: Nothing is pitched into the tank and the cellar waits for the population already on the fruit and in the building to start work. What is the trade being accepted?
opts: A faster and steadier ferment, with less aromatic character to show
More aromatic complexity, against a slower and less predictable ferment
Lower alcohol and deeper colour than a pitched culture gives
Higher alcohol, since the wild population tolerates more of it
exp: An ambient ferment is a succession of species rather than one strain, and the wine picks up more variety from that sequence. The risk is real: the ferment can crawl, stop short of dryness or throw volatile acidity, so the cellar has to be ready to step in.

q: Fermentation halts at four grams of sugar per litre in a vat that ran too hot, and the yeast are dead. Why is that dangerous rather than merely inconvenient?
opts: The wine will refuse to fall bright while any sugar remains in it
The four grams unbalance the red, since any sugar reads as sweetness
Sugar with no yeast working on it invites spoilage
The colour will drop out of solution within a matter of days
exp: A stuck ferment has to be protected with sulphur and restarted with a culture acclimatised to the alcohol already present, and the odds worsen the longer it sits. Heat, very high sugar and a shortage of nutrient in the juice are the usual causes.

q: Instead of a packet of dried yeast, a cellar picks a small quantity of grapes a week early, ferments them and tips the result into the main vat. What is that starter called?
opts: A dosage
A pied de cuve
A liqueur de tirage
A solera
exp: It gives the vineyard's own population a running start, so the main ferment begins promptly without a commercial strain ever entering the building. It sits between pitching a culture and waiting on the ambient flora entirely, and it carries some of the risk of both.

q: One Chardonnay ferments in barrel from the start; another ferments in steel and is racked into the same barrels afterwards. Which difference should show in the glass?
opts: The steel-fermented wine finishes higher in alcohol
The barrel-fermented wine carries its oak more seamlessly
The steel-fermented wine ends up deeper in colour
The barrel-fermented wine tastes markedly more oaky and obvious
exp: Fermenting in wood binds the oak compounds into the wine while the yeast are still active, and the sediment left behind keeps working on the texture afterwards, so the wine feels broader as well as less overtly oaky. Moving a finished wine into oak lays the flavour on top of it instead, which reads as a seasoning rather than as part of the wine.
